tweets.text:
Powerful quantum computers could pose a serious risk.

And preparing the world's infrastructure for quantum attacks will take longer than most people expect.

I came across this breakdown from @PaloAltoNtwks, and it got me thinking about how many systems we'd actually need to upgrade.

We're talking about:

→ Payment systems
→ Digital identities and authentication
→ Software updates and security checks
→ Older connected devices that may be difficult to update

With so much infrastructure to upgrade, I can see why NIST isn't waiting around. It finalized its first three quantum-resistant cryptography standards in 2024 and is already urging organizations to adopt them.

There's another concern, too.

Encrypted data stolen today could become readable years later, once quantum computers become powerful enough.

Lots of ground to cover, so best start early if you ask me.

Time to share a bit more about @StacysBrain – my new product that (I hope) will enter the market over the next couple of weeks.

What will it be?
MVP = an open, graded database of marketing insights and benchmarks – each with its own sample, methodology, age, and vendor interest data.

I told you about the pain (and I’m sure you know it yourself): AI often relies on outdated numbers or just hallucinates, and lots of marketing articles have zero proof or research behind them.

It’s like a circle jerk where people cross-cite each other. But once you try to find who was the first one to say something, it turns out there’s no source at all.

In some fields it’s probably fine.

In marketing, it’s a huge problem, because we invest money based on decisions that are often backed by low-quality research (or no research at all).

So I see Stacy's Brain as the fix.

We’ve been building this for the last 3 months, and the database will have 500+ insight cards (checked and vetted by my team) at release.

Very excited tbh.
Stay tuned <3

#Uranium #Silver #Copper #Gold

⚡ DAILY METALS PULSE — MONDAY, OCTOBER 12, 2026

New week. Inflation in focus. Nuclear investment gathering momentum.

☢️ URANIUM
Last week brought Google’s 20-year agreement for 890 MW of nuclear power from Constellation, alongside DOE’s conditional financing commitment of up to $4.2B for Vistra’s nuclear upgrades.
My take: more output from existing reactors strengthens the long-term fuel demand story. Watching whether uranium equities build on that momentum this week.

🥈 SILVER
Spot silver around $60.62 in late-morning trading. Wednesday’s US CPI could set the tone: softer inflation would help, while a stronger dollar remains a headwind. I’m watching whether silver can regain momentum alongside gold.

🔩 COPPER
LME copper traded above $14,600/t this morning as Chinese infrastructure stimulus hopes met fresh supply concerns in Chile. Centinela strike action and potential disruption at Escondida put mine supply firmly on this week’s watchlist.

🥇 GOLD
Gold around $4,171 after retreating from an early one-week high. The dollar is keeping pressure on bullion ahead of CPI Wednesday, followed by PPI and retail sales Thursday.

📌 WEEK AHEAD
Inflation data, the dollar, Chilean mine developments and follow-through in uranium equities.
TSX and TSXV are closed today for Canadian Thanksgiving, so Canadian mining stocks rejoin the action Tuesday.

My focus: how the metals respond to the data—and whether miners confirm the move. ⚒️

One of my main Snapchat investment theses comes from something very simple: talking to young people.

I’ve already written enough about the numbers, growth, and Evan Spiegel. Today I want to talk about something different.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴.

For those of you who haven’t used Snapchat, like myself, and don’t belong to the younger generation, it’s important to understand how it works.

In my generation, we communicated through phone calls.

The next generation moved to short voice notes. Then came text messages. WhatsApp and WhatsApp groups.

Now, the younger generation increasingly communicates through photos. Instead of telling you what they’re doing or how they’re feeling, they simply send a picture.

Communication is evolving from words to images.

$SNAP is the best platform to take a picture, select your friends, and send it to all of them at once. They respond with their own pictures. No need for long messages or explanations.

A picture says what you’re doing, how you feel, or what mood you’re in.

Something else I’ve noticed while traveling through Europe: young people seem less interested in showing off their lives and bodies on Instagram just to collect likes. They increasingly value privacy and communicating with real friends.

𝗦𝗻𝗮𝗽𝗰𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲.

A Pew Research Center study published in 2026 found that 57% of teenage Snapchat users message friends daily, more than on Instagram or TikTok. And 44% say Snapchat helps their friendships.

We all know how powerful teenage consumers are. Even when they don’t have money, they influence how their parents spend theirs.

Today, another young woman told me that she and many of her friends are returning to Snapchat after years of not using it.

Why? Because it’s simply the easiest way to communicate with friends.

𝗖𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘄𝗲 𝗯𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝗻𝗮𝗽𝗰𝗵𝗮𝘁?

Now consider the monetization opportunity.

Snapchat has nearly 1 billion monthly users and over 1 trillion saved Memories.

The company introduced paid storage above 5GB, starting at $1.99 per month.

Imagine just 50 million people paying $2 a month. That’s $1.2 billion in annual revenue.

The same young woman told me her friend would never pay for Instagram, but happily pays Snapchat to preserve eight years of memories.

𝗣𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗮, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗽𝗮𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀.

And here’s something Wall Street should pay attention to.

In February 2026, Snap announced over 25 million paying subscribers and more than $1 billion in annualized direct revenue.

𝗣𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗽𝗮𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝗻𝗮𝗽𝗰𝗵𝗮𝘁.

This is what I call One Up on Wall Street. Sometimes you learn more about a company by speaking with its customers than by reading another 100-page Wall Street report.

Of course, everything still depends on @evanspiegel. His ego, poor capital allocation, and what I consider his foolish pursuit of Specs without a partner could ruin this opportunity.

But the ingredients for a great turnaround are there.

Will it happen? I don’t know.

So why should it be so difficult for a company like $SNAP, which already has a working product that could bring AI into everyday life, to raise $1 billion at a $5 billion valuation?

The technology already exists. The product is already built. And the potential for further development is enormous.
AI needs a bridge to the physical world. AR glasses could be that bridge.

tweets.text:
One of my more controversial bets: the AI feed will be the form factor of 2027!

Most people don’t know what to prompt, and they won’t prompt their way into complicated agentic workflows. With chat, we ask users for digital labor: figure out what AI can do, explain the task, provide the context, repeat. That’s a lot to ask if we want billions of people using agents every day. 

Meanwhile, people already spend hours in feeds. Twitter, Instagram, LinkedIn. They know how to scroll, discover something useful, and act on it.

An intelligent system that knows you should bring you the next useful action. Here’s the email you need to answer, already drafted. Here are the latest sales numbers, with an update ready to send to your team. You approve, edit, dismiss, or jump into chat to go deeper. That’s how people will discover what agents can do, without having to invent a prompt first.

And you can put ads in a feed, one of the biggest business models on the internet. A system that understands your plans can recommend a relevant restaurant, product, or service, clearly labeled as sponsored. You get a reason to come back every day, useful work ready to approve, and a business model to fund the agents doing it.

The real SaaS apocalypse is pretty simple: every piece of software becomes reproducible. The cost of building it goes toward zero, competition becomes brutal, and eventually the price follows. Good luck charging for something anyone can recreate.

Computer use is the breakthrough here imo. Here’s how it works:

One agent navigates the existing software, clicks through every feature and documents everything in a markdown file. A swarm of agents builds it. Another agent acts as the verifier, opens the new software, clicks everywhere, checks that everything works, sends bugs back. Repeat.

I think this scenario is very possible and very much in the work. 

But people are missing the other side which is the bull case for big tech cos. 

If you’re Adobe, you already have a massive test suite documenting how the software is supposed to behave, including all the backend stuff you can’t discover by clicking around. You have insane usage telemetry, decades of customer feedback, and you know which obscure features people actually depend on.

You can build the same software factory. Except you start with a huge advantage.

Use the agents to clean up decades of legacy code. Make the software load faster, feel faster, break less. Give it clean APIs that agents can use. Then use your distribution to ship that better product to millions of existing customers.

Even if you burn $1M in tokens doing this, that’s roughly the annual cost of a handful of engineers in the Bay Area.

And getting the mass market to switch takes time. Especially in the enterprise. A free open-source alternative still has to earn trust, build credibility and convince people to move their workflows. “We cloned Photoshop” doesn’t automatically do that.

So there’s also a pretty strong bull case: the incumbents build the software factory first, use their tests, customer knowledge and distribution to move faster, and end up with better software, higher margins, more revenue and happier customers.

If they don’t move fast enough, well, we’re back to the bear case.
